segments.voice: Yesterday began Sanskrit sounds for readers with the plainest letter, a, the one Krishna names in the Gita, hidden in almost every consonant. Did you listen for the a inside it? Today, the same sound, held longer. Day one thousand forty-one.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `A: THE OPEN MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Write the name of the prince of Ayodhya in careful English letters and it looks like this: R, a with a small line over it, m, a. Rāma. The line sits on the first a only. The second a has nothing. It's a tiny mark, easy to treat as decoration, easy for the eye to slide right over. But it's an instruction about time. It tells the voice where to stay and where to move on. Today, the line over the letter.
screen: `RĀMA: A LINE OVER ONE A.` → `NOT DECORATION.` → `AN INSTRUCTION ABOUT TIME.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's Upanishad listed what the teaching of sound covers, and one item on that list was matra: length, the measure of a sound in time. Sanskrit vowels come in short and long pairs. Short a, long ā. Short i, long ī. Short u, long ū. In Devanagari the long vowel has its own letter or sign. In English transliteration, it gets a small line on top. So that line means: hold this one longer. The tradition of reciting measures this in units it calls matras: a short vowel takes one, a long vowel about two. Now listen to names you already know. Rāma: the first syllable long, the second short. Rah-muh. Sītā: both vowels long. See-tah. Gītā, as in the Bhagavad Gita: also both long, so the name ends on an open ah, not a clipped uh. And then words where nothing is long. Karma: both short. Kur-muh. Shiva: both short. Shi-vuh. Nothing is wrong with how English speakers say these names; anyone who hears them will know who you mean. But the length changes the music. Much Sanskrit verse is measured in light and heavy syllables, and vowel length helps decide which is which, so length is part of a line's rhythm, the way beats are part of a song. Stretch the wrong syllable and a chanted verse starts to limp. Get the lengths right and the line walks the way it was made to walk. That's why the little line matters to a reader. It isn't about sounding impressive. It's a way of hearing the text as its reciters heard it, one measured breath of sound after another.
screen: `MATRA: LENGTH, A SOUND'S MEASURE IN TIME.` · `SHORT A, LONG Ā. SHORT I, LONG Ī.` · `RĀMA, SĪTĀ, GĪTĀ. KARMA, SHIVA.` · `LENGTH IS PART OF THE RHYTHM.` · then, large: `THE LINE MEANS: STAY LONGER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and breathe in. On the out-breath, say a short a, quick and soft, then a long ā, held about twice as long. Breathe in. Do it again. Feel the difference in the body: one is a step, the other is a stride. Then try a name you know. Rāma: long, then short. Sītā: long, then long. Say each slowly, letting the line over the letter decide how long you stay. If you pray, you can let a name you pray with carry this rhythm. If not, just listen to the measure. The bell holds the time.
Matra. The length of a sound in time: short and long vowels, and the small line over a letter that means stay longer.
Your line: let one long vowel be long. Today, when you see a line over a letter, slow down on it, and let one long vowel be long. Day one thousand forty-one.

howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit learn short and long vowels as pairs, and reciters of verses keep the lengths carefully, since the rhythm of a verse depends on them.

notes: Editor pass: cut the unsupported 'most of the time' from the hook; replaced the garbled 'the people who carry them' with 'anyone who hears them'.
Day 2 of 7 in 'Sanskrit sounds for readers'.
'A short vowel takes one matra, a long about two' is stated as the tradition of recitation ('the tradition measures'), not from the cited text. Confirm wording.

Pronunciation guides (Rah-muh, See-tah, Kur-muh, Shi-vuh) are rough English approximations; final short a as 'uh' is standard in modern recitation. Confirm Śiva is short i, short a, and that Gītā has two long vowels.
'Sanskrit verse is built out of patterns of short and long syllables' is a general claim about meter, not from the cited text; a Keeper may prefer 'tradition says'.
Respect line: 'nothing is wrong with how English speakers say these names' is meant to avoid shaming anglicized pronunciations; confirm tone.

Audit pass: meter line corrected; classical meter counts light and heavy syllables (laghu/guru), where a short vowel before two consonants also counts heavy, so "built out of short and long syllables" was loose.
